title.en: Early humans and the beginning of civilisation

text.en: Thousands of years ago there were no books, no cities and no writing. How do we know about those people? Stones, bones, paintings and ruins tell the story.

Early humans lived by hunting animals and gathering plants. They made tools of stone and later learned to use fire.
Before writing, people communicated through gestures, speech, cave paintings and symbols.
Archaeology studies the past from material remains such as tools, pottery, bones and ruins.
Farming and animal rearing led to settled villages, a big change in human life.
Early civilisations grew along rivers, such as the Indus in the Indian subcontinent, the Nile in Egypt and the Tigris and Euphrates in Mesopotamia.
Their cities had planned streets, drains, trade and craft work. Writing was invented to keep records.
Civilisations interacted through trade. Indus beads and seals have been found in Mesopotamia.
Understanding the past helps us see how ideas and technologies spread across the world.

problem.en: Explain how archaeologists learn about people who left no writing.

text.en: They dig and study tools, pottery and houses.
They date objects and compare them across sites.
They then reconstruct how people lived.

prompt.en: Why did early civilisations grow near rivers?

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all early humans lived in cities

points.en: Farming led to settled life and cities.
Early civilisations traded with each other.
